```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE)
library(knitr)
is_pdf  <- knitr::is_latex_output()
is_html <- knitr::is_html_output()
# Table style for PDF tables (greyskull; "classic" changes nothing).
raisins_tstyle_knitr_hook(params$table_style)

# The PDF font twins (Caladea, Gelasio, ...) have no Greek glyphs, so in PDF
# Greek letters are written as LaTeX math, which renders in any font.
pdf_text <- function(x) {
  if (!is_pdf) return(x)
  x <- gsub("α", "$\\\\alpha$", x)
  x <- gsub("τ", "$\\\\tau$", x)
  x
}
pdf_cells <- function(d) {
  if (!is_pdf) return(d)
  for (j in seq_along(d)) if (is.character(d[[j]])) d[[j]] <- gsub("✔", "Yes", d[[j]])
  d
}

# p-values as text, so tiny values read "< 0.001" instead of rounding to 0.
p_cols <- function(d) {
  for (nm in grep("(^| )p$|p-value", names(d), value = TRUE)) if (is.numeric(d[[nm]]))
    d[[nm]] <- ifelse(is.na(d[[nm]]), "", ifelse(d[[nm]] < 0.001, "< 0.001", formatC(d[[nm]], digits = 3, format = "g")))
  d
}

tbl <- function(d, cap) {
  if (is.null(d) || !nrow(d)) return(invisible(NULL))
  d <- pdf_cells(p_cols(as.data.frame(d)))
  if (is_html) {
    print(kableExtra::kable_classic(
      kable(d, format = "html", caption = cap, row.names = FALSE),
      full_width = FALSE, html_font = params$font))
  } else if (is_pdf) {
    # LaTeX numbers captions itself ("Table 1:"), and HOLD_position keeps each
    # table where it is written instead of floating it to a later page.
    print(kableExtra::kable_styling(
      kable(d, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, caption = sub("^Table [0-9]+\\. ", "", cap), row.names = FALSE),
      latex_options = "HOLD_position"))
  } else {
    # Word: plain table; font and table style are applied to the .docx afterwards.
    print(kable(d, format = "pipe", caption = cap, row.names = FALSE))
  }
  cat("\n\n")
}
```

```{r method-flags, include=FALSE}
has <- function(x) !is.null(x) && NROW(x) > 0
has_plot <- !is.null(params$plot_path) && !is.na(params$plot_path) && file.exists(params$plot_path)
```

## 1. Methodology

The data are a yearly time series $Y_t$ observed at years $t_1 < t_2 < \dots < t_n$. Each selected series (for example area, production or yield) is analysed separately; when a group column is chosen, the series are first summed over groups for each year. Time is measured as $t = \text{year} - t_1$, so $t = 0$ in the first year.

```{asis, echo = has(params$growth)}
### 1.1 Growth rates

**Compound growth rate (CGR).** An exponential growth model is fitted to all years by ordinary least squares on the log scale:

$$\ln Y_t = a + b\,t + \varepsilon_t, \qquad \text{CGR}\,(\%) = \left(e^{b} - 1\right) \times 100 .$$

The CGR is the constant annual rate implied by the whole series. Its significance is the $t$-test of $H_0\!: b = 0$ (column *CGR p*). Only years with $Y_t > 0$ can be used.

**Compound annual growth rate (CAGR).** Uses only the first and last years:

$$\text{CAGR}\,(\%) = \left[\left(\frac{Y_{n}}{Y_{1}}\right)^{1/(t_n - t_1)} - 1\right] \times 100 .$$

It is simple to explain but depends heavily on the two end points.

**Average annual growth.** The mean of the year-on-year percentage changes, $\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{t=2}^{n} \frac{Y_t - Y_{t-1}}{Y_{t-1}} \times 100$.
```

```{asis, echo = has(params$trend)}
### 1.2 Trend fitting

Four trend models are fitted to each series:

| Model | Equation |
|:--|:--|
| Linear | $Y_t = a + b\,t$ |
| Quadratic | $Y_t = a + b\,t + c\,t^2$ |
| Cubic | $Y_t = a + b\,t + c\,t^2 + d\,t^3$ |
| Exponential | $\ln Y_t = a + b\,t$, i.e. $Y_t = A\,e^{b t}$ |

Models are ranked by the adjusted coefficient of determination, $\bar R^2 = 1 - (1 - R^2)\frac{n-1}{n-k-1}$, where $k$ is the number of terms besides the intercept; this penalises extra terms. The Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) is reported as a second guide (lower is better). The best model is drawn in the fitted-trend figure. Note that the exponential model's $\bar R^2$ is on the log scale.
```

```{asis, echo = has(params$mk)}
### 1.3 Mann-Kendall trend test and Sen's slope

The Mann-Kendall test (Mann, 1945; Kendall, 1975) is a non-parametric test for a monotonic trend; it does not assume a straight line or normally distributed errors. The test statistic is

$$S = \sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\sum_{j=i+1}^{n} \operatorname{sgn}\left(Y_j - Y_i\right),$$

with variance, corrected for $g$ groups of tied values of size $t_p$,

$$\operatorname{Var}(S) = \frac{n(n-1)(2n+5) - \sum_{p=1}^{g} t_p (t_p - 1)(2 t_p + 5)}{18}.$$

The standardised statistic is $Z = (S - 1)/\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(S)}$ if $S > 0$, $Z = 0$ if $S = 0$ and $Z = (S + 1)/\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(S)}$ if $S < 0$, with a two-sided $p$-value from the standard normal distribution. Kendall's $\tau = S \big/ \left[n(n-1)/2\right]$ ranges from $-1$ (always falling) to $+1$ (always rising).

**Sen's slope** (Sen, 1968) is the median of all pairwise slopes, $Q = \operatorname{median}\left\{(Y_j - Y_i)/(t_j - t_i) : i < j\right\}$, a robust estimate of the change per year in the units of the series. Its confidence interval uses the ordered slopes at ranks $(N - C_\alpha)/2$ and $(N + C_\alpha)/2$, where $N$ is the number of pairs and $C_\alpha = z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(S)}$.

The test assumes the yearly observations are independent; strong serial correlation can make a trend look more significant than it is.
```

```{asis, echo = has(params$instab)}
### 1.4 Instability

The coefficient of variation, $\text{CV}\,(\%) = s / \bar Y \times 100$, measures total variability, including the part caused by the trend itself. The Cuddy-Della Valle Index (Cuddy and Della Valle, 1978) removes the trend using the adjusted $\bar R^2$ of the linear trend:

$$\text{CDVI}\,(\%) = \text{CV} \times \sqrt{1 - \bar R^2}.$$

A CDVI below 15% is read as low instability, 15% to 30% as moderate, and above 30% as high instability.
```

```{asis, echo = has(params$decomp)}
### 1.5 Area-yield decomposition

Production is area times yield, $P = A \times Y$, with yield computed as $P/A$. The change between the first (0) and last (1) year is split additively:

$$\Delta P = \underbrace{Y_0\,\Delta A}_{\text{area effect}} + \underbrace{A_0\,\Delta Y}_{\text{yield effect}} + \underbrace{\Delta A\,\Delta Y}_{\text{interaction}},$$

so the three effects always add up to the total change in production.
```
